These standards apply across all typography tokens and components that display text.

sub_skills.skill_content: Custom fonts need to be downloaded before they can be displayed, especially on the web. Make sure that you have sensible fallbacks and fast loading time for your typography assets. Using system fonts solves this performance problem.

rsc.title: Performance
rsc.content: Custom fonts need to be downloaded before they can be displayed, especially on the web. Make sure that you have sensible fallbacks and fast loading time for your typography assets. Using system fonts solves this performance problem.

sub_skills.skill_content: In the context of design tokens, accessibility refers to ensuring that color and other visual choices meet contrast and legibility standards, such as WCAG guidelines, for users with visual impairments. It means checking that text colors have sufficient contrast against their backgrounds and that icon sizes remain legible at small scales. Accessibility considerations get baked into the tokens themselves so every component built from them meets the same baseline.

User onboarding encompasses the design patterns and instructional elements that guide new users through an interface to help them understand its core value and functionality. These guidelines define how tooltips, walkthroughs, empty state illustrations, and progress indicators should look and behave to ensure a consistent experience across the product. By establishing clear standards for welcoming users, teams create intuitive pathways that reduce friction and improve product adoption.

Microcopy guidelines provide a standardized framework for writing the small snippets of text that appear throughout an interface, such as button labels, error messages, and tooltips. These instructions outline the preferred voice, tone, vocabulary, and formatting standards to ensure that all user-facing text is clear, concise, and helpful.

rsc.title: Microcopy Guidelines
rsc.content: Microcopy guidelines provide a standardized framework for writing the small snippets of text that appear throughout an interface, such as button labels, error messages, and tooltips. These instructions outline the preferred voice, tone, vocabulary, and formatting standards to ensure that all user-facing text is clear, concise, and helpful.

sub_skills.skill_content: For icons that convey a meaning or serve a function, add the necessary support for screen readers. You can skip this for decorative icons.

rsc.title: Accessibility
rsc.content: For icons that convey a meaning or serve a function, add the necessary support for screen readers. You can skip this for decorative icons.

sub_skills.skill_content: In iconography, style refers to the consistent visual approach used across a set of icons, such as outlined, filled, or duotone, along with consistent stroke width and corner treatment. Keeping a single style across all icons prevents a product from feeling visually disjointed when icons from different sources get mixed together. Style guidelines usually specify exact stroke widths and corner radii to keep new icons consistent with existing ones.

rsc.title: Style
rsc.content: In iconography, style refers to the consistent visual approach used across a set of icons, such as outlined, filled, or duotone, along with consistent stroke width and corner treatment. Keeping a single style across all icons prevents a product from feeling visually disjointed when icons from different sources get mixed together. Style guidelines usually specify exact stroke widths and corner radii to keep new icons consistent with existing ones.

sub_skills.skill_content: Naming conventions for icons define how each icon file or component is labeled, typically based on what it represents or the action it performs, such as "icon-search" or "icon-trash." Consistent naming makes icons easier to find and reference in code, especially as an icon set grows to hundreds of entries. Design systems usually document a naming pattern to avoid duplicate or ambiguous icon names.

rsc.title: Naming

Consistent naming makes icons easier to find and reference in code, especially as an icon set grows to hundreds of entries. Design systems usually document a naming pattern to avoid duplicate or ambiguous icon names.

sub_skills.skill_content: Draw your icons in a bounding box that plays well with your grid. This makes for a better pairing with other UI elements. A good example of this would be icons with bounding boxes paired with text.

rsc.title: Grid Relation
rsc.content: Draw your icons in a bounding box that plays well with your grid. This makes for a better pairing with other UI elements. A good example of this would be icons with bounding boxes paired with text.

sub_skills.skill_content: Icon sizes define the standard dimensions an icon set supports, such as 16px, 24px, and 32px, so icons remain crisp and consistent wherever they appear. Design systems typically build icons on a fixed grid at each supported size to keep stroke widths and proportions consistent across the set. Components reference these standard sizes rather than scaling icons arbitrarily.

rsc.title: Sizes
rsc.content: Icon sizes define the standard dimensions an icon set supports, such as 16px, 24px, and 32px, so icons remain crisp and consistent wherever they appear. Design systems typically build icons on a fixed grid at each supported size to keep stroke widths and proportions consistent across the set. Components reference these standard sizes rather than scaling icons arbitrarily.

An icon representing a trash can might include keywords like "delete," "remove," and "bin" so it surfaces under multiple search terms. Well-chosen keywords reduce duplicate icon requests when someone can't find an existing icon that already covers their need.

By documenting these variations, teams can establish a clear baseline of the current design state and prioritize the necessary cleanup or standardization required for the new design system.

sub_skills.skill_content: SEO stands for Search Engine Optimization. It is the practice of improving a website so that search engines like Google can find it, understand it, and show it to people searching for related topics. The goal is discoverability and retrieval: making sure your content shows up when someone searches for something you cover.

GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization. It is the practice of making content visible inside AI-generated answers, such as those produced by ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, or Perplexity. Unlike SEO, which targets a list of ranked links, GEO targets the retrieval systems that AI models pull from when generating a response.

sub_skills.skill_content: Semantic search is a method of finding relevant content based on meaning rather than exact keyword matches. It allows a system to understand that "cheap flights" and "affordable plane tickets" refer to the same idea. This is the foundation that lets modern search and AI systems retrieve relevant content even when the wording differs from the query.

sub_skills.skill_content: Lexical search matches the literal words in a query against the literal words in a document, similar to a find-and-replace function. Vector search instead converts text into numerical representations and matches based on meaning, so it can find relevant content even when no exact words overlap. Most modern retrieval systems, including those used by AI models, combine both methods rather than relying on just one.

sub_skills.skill_content: Hybrid search combines lexical and vector search in a single system, so it can catch exact matches, like product names or error codes, while also catching content that means the same thing but uses different words. This combination generally performs better than either method alone, since lexical search alone misses paraphrased content and vector search alone misses exact terms.

skills.skill_content: Search engines function as massive indexing systems that constantly crawl the internet to discover, analyze, and store web content. They use automated software bots, often called spiders or crawlers, to follow links from page to page, gathering information to add to their vast databases. Once this data is collected, complex algorithms evaluate the content based on various factors to determine its relevance and quality, ultimately organizing it so that the most helpful results can be retrieved instantly when a user enters a search query.

rsc.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
How Google and Search Engines Work

sub_skills.skill_content: Search engines function by using automated programs called spiders or crawlers to scan the internet, discover web pages, and follow links from one site to another. Once these pages are found, the information is processed and stored in a massive database known as an index, where it is categorized based on content and relevance. When a user performs a search, the engine retrieves the most suitable results from this index and orders them according to complex algorithms that determine which pages best answer the user's query.

sub_skills.skill_content: Retrieval is the step where a search or AI system pulls a set of candidate documents that might answer a query, based on relevance matching. sub_skills.skill_content: Personalization is when search results differ based on an individual user's history, preferences, or device. Localization is when results differ based on geographic location, showing nearby businesses or region-specific content. Both mean that search results are not a single fixed list, but vary depending on who is searching and from where.

Training data is the information an AI model learned from during its initial training process, baked into the model itself and not updated in real time. Grounding refers to an AI system retrieving current, external information at the moment it answers a question, rather than relying only on what it learned during training. A model can generate an answer purely from training data, purely from grounded retrieval, or a mix of both, and knowing which is happening matters for understanding why a system cites certain sources.

sub_skills.skill_content: Embeddings are numerical representations of text that capture its meaning, allowing a computer to compare how similar two pieces of text are. Chunking is the process of splitting a long document into smaller pieces before it gets indexed for retrieval. Systems typically search and retrieve at the chunk level rather than the whole-document level, since a smaller, focused piece of text is easier to match accurately to a specific question. How a document gets chunked can affect whether the right piece of information gets found and cited.

sub_skills.skill_content: WP-CLI is a command-line interface for WordPress. It allows you to manage WordPress installations, update plugins and themes, publish posts, and perform many other administrative tasks without using a web browser. It's a powerful tool for developers and system administrators who need to automate WordPress management.

sub_skills.skill_content: Bedrock is a WordPress boilerplate project designed to improve WordPress development by utilizing modern development standards. It introduces a more structured project setup, dependency management with Composer, and environment configuration, making WordPress projects more maintainable, secure, and easier to deploy. It essentially treats your WordPress site as a modern application.

sub_skills.skill_content: Sage is a WordPress starter theme that offers a modern development workflow. It utilizes tools like Composer, Webpack, and Blade templating to streamline the process of building custom WordPress themes. This approach aims to improve code quality, maintainability, and overall development efficiency.

sub_skills.skill_content: Composer is a tool for managing dependencies in PHP projects, including WordPress. It lets you declare the libraries your project needs, and it will install them for you. This means you can easily include external code, like plugins or themes from repositories, without manually downloading and managing the files. Composer simplifies updating these dependencies and ensures your project has the correct versions of everything it needs to run.

skills.skill_content: Accessibility refers to designing and developing websites that are usable by people of all abilities, including those with disabilities. This involves ensuring that content is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust for users who may rely on assistive technologies like screen readers, keyboard navigation, or alternative input devices. A focus on accessibility creates a more inclusive and user-friendly experience for everyone.

rsc.title: How to Make Your WordPress Website Accessible

skills.skill_content: WordPress Coding Standards are a set of guidelines and best practices for writing code that is consistent, readable, and maintainable within the WordPress ecosystem. These standards cover various aspects of coding, including PHP, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and aim to ensure that code is easy to understand, debug, and collaborate on, regardless of who wrote it. Adhering to these standards helps create a more unified and professional codebase for WordPress themes, plugins, and the core software itself.
